Zambia’s Semiconductor Tariff Plan Sparks Production Slowdown and Industry Uncertainty

Zambia’s new 20% import tariff on finished semiconductors, announced by the Ministry of Trade earlier this month, is sending ripples through the country’s nascent semiconductor manufacturing sector. The measure, which took effect on June 1, is intended to encourage domestic value addition but has already led to production slowdowns and operational uncertainty at several industry sites.

Firms such as Lusaka Microfabrication and Copperbelt Semicon Assemblies report that the tariff is impacting their ability to import essential finished chips for integrated testing and packaging operations. “Our supply chain has tightened considerably, with the cost of finished chips rising overnight,” said Charles Tembo, operations director at Lusaka Microfabrication. “We have had to reduce our output and temporarily cut back on shift hours for around 70 workers at our Lusaka plant.”

Industry analysts warn that the measure could have unintended consequences for Zambia’s semiconductor ambitions. “These tariffs risk undermining local firms’ competitiveness, particularly those relying on hybrid production models,” said Grace Mwansa, sector analyst at TechTrade Africa. She noted that several sites in Lusaka and Ndola have reported delays in scheduled projects and a slowdown in hiring.

The Zambia Semiconductor Industry Association (ZSIA) has called for urgent dialogue with the government. “While we support the goal of building Zambia’s semiconductor capabilities, the speed and scale of these tariffs are disrupting ongoing operations and jeopardizing jobs,” said ZSIA chairperson John Phiri. According to the association, more than 300 workers across the sector have seen their hours reduced or contracts suspended since the tariffs took effect.

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Trade said the policy remains under review and consultations with industry stakeholders are ongoing. Meanwhile, semiconductor firms are closely monitoring the situation and adapting operations as the effects of the new tariffs continue to unfold.
